strengths: The paper conducts an unusually thorough empirical investigation: exhaustive grid searches over learning rate, batch size, and clipping bound across three datasets (SUN397, Cassava, CIFAR-100, plus a 10% subset), two backbones plus ResNet-50, multiple privacy budgets, epoch counts, and multiple seeds. This level of tuning rigor is necessary to expose the hyperparameter interactions being studied and is rarely done in DP-ML papers.

The central finding—that the optimal clipping bound C can increase under tighter privacy (smaller ε) and less capable backbones, contradicting theory-based heuristics (C* ∝ 1/σ³ from Koloskova et al.)—is counterintuitive, clearly demonstrated (Figs. 1-2), and mechanistically explained via gradient norm distribution shifts (Fig. 3).

Theorem 5.1 (exact MSE-optimal clipping constant for a fixed minibatch) is a clean, novel result (the authors correctly position it against Amin et al. 2019) that explains why C* depends on the gradient distribution and not just σ, and it usefully reconciles theory with the empirical observations.

The re-weighting interpretation of clipping (Section 5.3, Fig. 4) is a useful conceptual lens that yields testable predictions, e.g., correctly predicting when noise-free-C-tuning (Ponomareva et al.) and automatic clipping (AUTO-S) fail; the AUTO-S comparison (Fig. 5, Table A3) directly validates these predictions on hard datasets under tight privacy.

The batch-size analysis correctly identifies that fixed-steps guidance (per-step effective noise σ²/q² sweet spot) fails in the fixed-epochs setting and proposes cumulative noise σ√T plus a minimum-steps constraint as a better predictor, with supporting evidence across datasets and epoch counts (Figs. 6-7, A13-A15).

Clear writing, well-organized related work covering contradictory prior recommendations, and a transparent LLM-usage disclosure. Reproducibility appears good: standard libraries (Opacus, timm), detailed hyperparameter grids, and hardware specified.
weaknesses: Narrow experimental scope: all experiments use parameter-efficient fine-tuning (FiLM, ~0.5-1.5% trainable parameters) for image classification. The claim that results transfer to full-model tuning and other domains (e.g., LLMs) is asserted but not tested; gradient norm distributions under full fine-tuning could differ qualitatively.

The theoretical contribution, while correct and useful, is modest: Theorem 5.1 is a deterministic one-shot MSE analysis that ignores minibatch sampling noise, optimizer dynamics, and the fact that C* itself depends on the gradient distribution being shifted by training under the chosen C. It is an explanatory device rather than an actionable recipe for choosing C.

The proposed batch-size rule is qualitative: 'minimize batch size subject to minimum steps and near-optimal cumulative noise' lacks a precise algorithm, the minimum-steps threshold is dataset-specific, and the paper does not quantitatively benchmark the rule's predictions against actual optima across all settings (evidence is largely visual via heatmaps).

Some findings partially reconfirm prior observations: McKenna et al. (2025) already noted smaller physical batches performing better in high-noise settings, and Räisä et al. (2024) already characterized the asymptotic batch-size behavior; the novelty lies mainly in the fixed-epochs framing and the clipping-side analysis.

Only DP-Adam is studied in depth; conclusions about optimizer-independent mechanisms would be strengthened by DP-SGD comparisons in the main analysis, and learning-rate/C/B interactions (e.g., the √B scaling note) are only briefly touched upon despite being acknowledged as important.

The 'learning-problem difficulty' construct is informal; it conflates privacy budget, backbone capability, and data scarcity without a formal definition, which slightly weakens the generality of the claims built on it.

strengths: Extensive and systematic experimental grid search over learning rate, clipping bound, and batch size across multiple datasets, models, and privacy budgets, with per-configuration tuning of learning rates to isolate effects
The central empirical observation—that the optimal clipping bound can increase under tighter privacy, contradicting existing theory—is interesting and clearly demonstrated (Fig. 2, Fig. 3)
The re-parameterization argument (Appendix B) clarifying the equivalence of normalized and unnormalized DP updates is useful for readers

The framing of clipping as gradient re-weighting of easy vs. hard classes is an insightful lens, and connects the results to the failure modes of practical methods like automatic clipping (Bu et al., 2023)
The fixed-epochs vs. fixed-steps distinction for batch size selection is a practically relevant observation that reconciles seemingly contradictory prior recommendations
weaknesses: Limited scope and generality: all experiments are on parameter-efficient fine-tuning (FiLM, ~1% of parameters) for image classification with three datasets; the claims in the conclusion about transferring to full-model tuning and other domains (e.g., LLMs) are speculative and unsupported

The theoretical contribution (Theorem 5.1) is modest: it is an implicit, fixed-minibatch MSE characterization where C* appears on both sides (C* depends on I_C which depends on C*), and it provides no convergence or utility guarantee; its explanatory power for the empirical findings is argued informally rather than validated quantitatively

There is a mismatch between the analysis setting (unnormalized DP noise scaling with C, ignoring minibatch sampling noise) and the experimental setting (normalized variant), which weakens the claimed theory–experiment connection; the paper asserts equivalence of the two variants but the noise-sensitivity analysis does not transfer directly

The batch-size 'rule' (minimum steps plus minimizing batch size under near-optimal cumulative noise σ√T) is heuristic, not a formal procedure; it is presented post hoc against the same experiments used to motivate it, with no prospective validation on new datasets or tasks

Several 'explanations' (e.g., gradient distributions shifting upward under tighter privacy, backbone capability acting like an effective ε change) are correlational observations from plots rather than validated causal mechanisms; no controlled experiments isolate these effects

Some experimental gaps: no comparison against adaptive clipping (Andrew et al., 2021) despite discussing its failure modes; the AUTO-S comparison uses only 3 seeds and one model/dataset regime; the 10%-CIFAR-100 results shown in the appendix are weakly connected to the main narrative

Impact is likely limited to practitioners of DP image fine-tuning; the findings largely confirm intuitions practitioners might already hold (e.g., 'tune C and B per task'), and no actionable general-purpose tuning method is proposed

Writing issues: minor grammatical errors (e.g., 'across of number of datasets'), Figures 6 and 7 are dense and difficult to parse, and the derivation of Eq. (2) from Koloskova et al. involves several unstated simplifications (dropping terms as 'not relevant') that deserve more careful justification

strengths: Thorough and well-designed empirical study: an exhaustive grid search over learning rate, clipping bound, and batch size across three datasets, multiple backbones (ViT-Tiny/Base, ResNet-50), multiple privacy budgets (ε from 0.25 to 8), and compute budgets, with multiple seeds—this level of hyperparameter sweep is necessary for the claims made and rarely done at this scale.

Clear and practically relevant message: the paper shows that fixed (C, B) defaults used in much of the DP literature (e.g., C=1) can be systematically suboptimal, and identifies when (tight privacy, weaker backbones, limited compute, imbalanced data).

The 'clipping as gradient re-weighting' analysis (Fig. 4) provides a mechanistic explanation connecting optimal clipping to per-class difficulty, and nicely explains when automatic clipping (Bu et al., 2023) and non-private C-selection heuristics (Ponomareva et al., 2023) fail.

The fixed-epochs vs. fixed-steps distinction for batch size selection is a genuinely useful reframing; the cumulative noise σ√T plus minimum-steps analysis explains why existing per-step signal-to-noise guidance fails under bounded compute.

The paper honestly positions itself against prior theory (Koloskova et al., 2023), derives its own MSE-optimal clipping characterization (Theorem 5.1), and includes careful appendices covering the normalized/unnormalized DP-Adam equivalence, exact grids, and datasets. LLM usage is transparently disclosed.

Experiments are mostly internally consistent with the theoretical reasoning (e.g., gradient norm distributions shifting upward under tighter privacy in Fig. 3, AUTO-S under-performing on hard datasets in Fig. 5/Table A3).
weaknesses: Theorem 5.1 is less strong than advertised: it is an implicit fixed-point characterization (C* appears on both sides via IC, GC, NC), derived per-minibatch under strong simplifications (no sampling noise, isotropic Gaussian noise, fixed gradient directions). It is also a fairly straightforward MSE minimization; calling it 'novel optimal clipping of independent interest' overstates its depth. Its connection to actual learning dynamics (as opposed to one-step gradient MSE) is heuristic.

There is some circularity in the empirical explanation: gradient norm distributions (Fig. 3) are measured after training with a given configuration, so the shift in norms is partly an effect of the training regime itself, not only of ε; the paper does not fully disentangle this.

Scope is narrow: all experiments use FiLM parameter-efficient fine-tuning for image classification on three datasets. The claim that the mechanisms 'transfer to full-model tuning' and to other modalities/LLMs is untested speculation. Given the practical framing, at least one full fine-tuning or text experiment would significantly strengthen the paper.

Effect sizes are sometimes small: on CIFAR-100 the tuned-vs-AUTO-S differences are 0.001–0.005 accuracy, and several Δ-accuracy plots in the appendix have magnitudes comparable to seed variation; the practical significance of 'fixed hyperparameters are suboptimal' varies a lot across settings, and the paper could be clearer about when the effect is material.

The proposed batch-size selection guidance (minimum steps + minimize batch size subject to near-optimal cumulative noise) remains a qualitative heuristic. It is not formalized as an algorithm, not validated out-of-sample on a new dataset/task, and its 'minimum number of steps' (e.g., 20 steps) is dataset-specific without a principled way to set it.

Some writing/presentation issues: the fixed-point notation in Theorem 5.1 is confusing; results in Fig. 2 that 'slightly help easy classes' rest on small margins; minor typos (e.g., 'across of number of datasets'); several key results (e.g., learning-rate √B scaling) are only mentioned in passing in the discussion without supporting analysis.

strengths: Systematic and extensive empirical study: the paper sweeps learning rate, batch size, and clipping bound jointly across multiple datasets (SUN397, CIFAR-100 and a 10% subset, Cassava, 20 Newsgroups), backbones (ViT-Tiny/Base, ResNet-50, DistilBERT, WRN), and training regimes (FiLM, LoRA, full fine-tuning, DP-SGD, from-scratch), which is unusually thorough for this area and necessary to expose subtle hyperparameter interactions.

Clear and practically useful identification of a theory–practice mismatch: tighter privacy empirically favors a larger clipping bound, contrary to common intuition, and the authors provide a mechanistic explanation via gradient norm distribution shifts and a clipping-as-reweighting view (retained weight analysis per class), connecting to fairness/disparate-impact concerns.

New theoretical results of independent interest: Theorem 5.2 derives the MSE-optimal clipping constant (exact MSE for the Gaussian mechanism, not just an upper bound), and Theorems 5.4/Corollary 5.5 connect per-step gradient MSE to optimization progress via a smoothness argument; the theory is used to qualitatively explain rather than overclaim about the experiments.

Novel and useful batch-size analysis under bounded compute (fixed epochs): the paper shows that existing fixed-steps heuristics (per-step signal-to-noise sweet spot) fail in this setting and proposes cumulative noise (σ√T) plus a minimum-steps constraint as an effective predictor of the optimal batch size, with consistent evidence across datasets and epoch budgets.

Honest scoping and transparent reporting: limitations are acknowledged (e.g., full fine-tuning behaves differently and the explanation is speculative), the LLM usage statement is thorough, and hyperparameter grids are fully documented, aiding reproducibility.

Findings directly challenge the widespread practice of fixing C and B across tasks/privacy levels (e.g., C=1 in De et al. 2022 and follow-ups), and provide concrete tuning guidance (Table 1), which is valuable to both practitioners and the many papers that cite DP-Adam default settings.
weaknesses: Theoretical contributions are relatively incremental: Theorem 5.2 is a per-step bias–variance decomposition of clipping plus Gaussian noise, and Theorem 5.4 is a standard smooth-descent argument; both rely on strong simplifying assumptions (no sampling noise, no mini-batch noise, gt = ∇L exactly, constant gradient directions), and the derived C* depends on unknown quantities, so it is descriptive rather than predictive and cannot be used as an actual tuning rule.

The batch-size guidance is heuristic and partly post-hoc: the cumulative-noise 'plateau' is an empirical observation, the required minimum number of steps is dataset-dependent and must be found by inspection (e.g., 20 steps on CIFAR-100, different on SUN397), and no procedure is validated on held-out tasks to show it selects near-optimal batch sizes a priori.

The central concept of 'learning-problem difficulty' is informal and never precisely defined or quantified; the paper asserts it is 'mainly governed by' privacy budget, data, compute, and backbone capability, but the evidence for this ordering is anecdotal rather than a validated predictor.

Magnitude of practical gains varies and is sometimes small: on 20 Newsgroups and CIFAR-100 at loose privacy, differences between clipping bounds are within roughly the seed-to-seed noise (fractions of a percent), and the practical impact of the recommendations is most compelling only in the hard regimes.

Generalizability is limited by scope: experiments are classification-only, dominated by parameter-efficient fine-tuning; the full fine-tuning regime contradicts the headline pattern and the offered explanation (parameter count → larger gradient norms) is speculative with no supporting measurements of gradient norms versus trainable-parameter count.

Statistical rigor is mixed: 3–5 seeds with min–max bands is on the light side for claims of small accuracy differences, and some retained-weight/gradient-distribution analyses (e.g., Fig. 4) use a single seed.
No public code release is stated, which weakens reproducibility for a paper whose primary contribution is a broad empirical characterization.

Positioning relative to closest prior work (Koloskova et al. 2023; Räisä et al. 2024; McKenna et al. 2025) is good, but some empirical observations (e.g., tighter privacy favoring larger effective batch/clipping trade-offs) overlap with recent concurrent findings, somewhat reducing novelty.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically relevant and underexplored question: how the optimal clipping bound C and batch size B vary across privacy budgets, backbone capability, and compute budgets in DP transfer learning, challenging the common practice of fixing (C, B) across tasks.

The experimental scope is genuinely extensive: multiple datasets (SUN397, Cassava, CIFAR-100, 20 Newsgroups), multiple backbones (ViT-Tiny/Base, ResNet-50, DistilBERT, WRN-16-4), multiple training regimes (FiLM, LoRA, DP-SGD, from scratch, full fine-tune), joint tuning of learning rate, batch size, and clipping bound, with multiple seeds.

The gradient re-weighting interpretation of clipping (Eq. 3, retained weight analysis) is an insightful lens that concretely connects clipping bounds to per-class performance disparities and explains why small C hurts hard classes.

The demonstration that existing batch-size selection heuristics (per-step noise sweet spot) fail under fixed-epoch compute constraints, and that cumulative noise plus a minimum-steps constraint better explains empirical optima, is a useful correction to prior guidance (Ponomareva et al., 2023; Räisä et al., 2024).
The comparison against automatic clipping (AUTO-S) supports the paper's narrative and clarifies when hyperparameter-free methods underperform.
Honest disclosure of LLM usage and clear description of experimental protocols.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is incremental and largely descriptive. Theorem 5.2 is a straightforward first-order optimality condition of the MSE between clipped-noisy and true gradients; Theorem 5.4 is a standard smoothness-based descent argument. The authors themselves admit C* cannot be computed without access to actual gradients, so the theory yields no actionable selection procedure — it only retroactively explains the observed phenomena.

There is a substantial gap between the analyzed setting and the experiments: the analysis assumes full-batch (no sampling noise), gradient descent, and the unnormalized DP-SGD variant, while all experiments use DP-Adam with Poisson subsampling and a normalized update. The claimed equivalence in Appendix B helps, but the mismatch in noise structure and optimizer dynamics is never bridged rigorously.

The central organizing concept, 'learning-problem difficulty', remains informal. No quantitative, measurable proxy for difficulty is proposed, so the practical guidance in Table 1 ('Try larger C', 'Increase C, decrease B') is qualitative and cannot be operationalized without the very grid search the paper says is necessary.

The proposed batch-size rule (minimum number of steps + minimizing batch under near-optimal cumulative noise) is validated only descriptively on existing results. There is no prospective experiment showing that applying the rule to a new dataset/setting selects a batch size achieving near-best accuracy, which is the real test of a selection rule.

Key comparisons with relevant baselines are missing: no empirical evaluation of adaptive clipping (Andrew et al., 2021) or error-feedback methods (Zhang et al., 2024), which are the most direct practical alternatives to tuned fixed C.

Several important conclusions rest on speculation rather than evidence, e.g., the explanation for why full fine-tuning prefers abnormally large C ('we speculate'), and speculation about how accuracy differences would grow on harder text tasks.

The claim that 'the number of epochs explains the compute quite well' is asserted without justification (e.g., wall-clock or per-sample-gradient compute costs, which are known to differ), and some experiments use 8 epochs, a very short budget whose external validity for realistic DP training is unclear.
No explicit code release or reproducibility statement is provided in the main paper, which limits confidence in reproducing such a compute-heavy grid search.
Some figures (e.g., Fig. 4, Fig. 1) are dense and hard to parse, and axis ranges/color scales are inconsistent across panels, making cross-setting comparisons harder than they should be.

The fixed-epochs framing, while motivated by limited compute, is a somewhat narrow scope: much of the DP literature operates under fixed-step budgets, and the paper does not characterize when each budget model is more appropriate.

strengths: Systematic and extensive empirical study: the paper covers multiple datasets (SUN397, CIFAR-100 including a low-data subset, Cassava, 20 Newsgroups), multiple architectures (ViT-Tiny/Base, ResNet-50, DistilBERT, WideResNet), multiple training regimes (FiLM, LoRA, full fine-tuning, from-scratch, DP-SGD vs DP-Adam), and jointly tunes learning rate, clipping bound, and batch size with carefully documented grids (Table A1). This level of thoroughness is unusual and lends credibility to the central claims.

The paper identifies and rigorously documents a genuinely counterintuitive phenomenon (tighter privacy can favor a larger clipping bound) and reconciles it with prior contradictory claims in the literature, which is a valuable service to the DP deep learning community.

The theoretical analysis is sound and supports the empirical findings: Theorem 5.2 gives a closed-form MSE-optimal clipping condition showing that C* depends jointly on the noise level and the gradient norm distribution (explaining why tighter privacy/less capable backbones shift optimal C upward), and Theorem 5.4/Corollary 5.5 connect minimizing per-step gradient MSE to per-step optimization progress. The proofs in Appendix E appear correct.

The 'clipping as gradient re-weighting' perspective (Eq. 3, Fig. 4) provides an intuitive, testable mechanism that explains when noise-free-tuning approaches (Ponomareva et al., 2023) and automatic clipping (Bu et al., 2023) succeed or fail; the predictions are verified experimentally (Fig. 5, Table A4).

The cumulative-noise analysis for batch size in the fixed-epochs setting is a useful practical contribution: it explains why existing fixed-steps heuristics fail (Fig. 6) and gives actionable guidance (minimum steps + flat region of cumulative noise) summarized in Table 1.

The paper is honest about the limits of its findings (e.g., full fine-tuning behaving differently, Section I.3; footnoted caveats about not claiming smaller C is never better for smaller epsilon), and the LLM usage disclosure in Appendix A is transparent and responsible.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than groundbreaking. Theorem 5.4 is essentially a standard smoothness-based descent lemma combined with a bias-variance decomposition, and Theorem 5.2, while neat, is a straightforward first-order-optimality condition of the MSE. Related analysis exists (Amin et al., 2019; Koloskova et al., 2023; Räisä et al., 2024), so the theoretical contribution is incremental, though the paper is transparent about this positioning.

The batch-size guidance is largely descriptive and post-hoc. The paper shows that cumulative noise and a minimum-step constraint correlate with optimal batch size (Figs. 6-7, A16, A35-A36), but does not validate the rule prospectively on new datasets/settings, nor does it quantify the practical gains a practitioner would obtain by following Table 1 versus common defaults.

Scope limitations: the headline findings are established mainly in the FiLM parameter-efficient fine-tuning regime on classification tasks; the full fine-tuning regime contradicts the difficulty-dependence story and is only speculatively explained via gradient norm magnitude (Section I.3). Other tasks (generation, detection, more modalities) are not covered, so generality of the central claim could be challenged.

Some experimental differences are small relative to the grid-search cost: e.g., on CIFAR-100 the accuracy gaps between clipping bounds and between AUTO-S and tuned C are tiny (Table A4), raising questions about practical significance in easy regimes, although gaps on SUN397/Cassava under tight privacy are meaningful.

Presentation issues: the main-text figures (Fig. 1 heatmaps, Fig. 7) are dense and hard to parse without reading the appendix; there are multiple language/typos and labeling errors (e.g., 'opter for', 'leads at it bets to', Figure A14's top/bottom panel descriptions appear swapped, 'ViT-Hard' in Fig. A22 caption, inconsistent epsilon values across some captions), which detract from polish.

Fixed δ=10^-5 throughout and ε ranges limited to ≳0.25; results at much tighter privacy regimes are not explored, and the compute-budget definition (epochs) ignores wall-clock differences across batch sizes (e.g., full-batch Poisson sampling costs), which slightly weakens the 'fixed compute' framing.
